answer: Use the operational-mode command set-alarm-state [state=]<value> [[acknowledge-text=]<value>] (all-alarms | [alarm-id-list=]<value>[,<value>]*). state is mandatory and takes an operator-state value of none, ack or close. Use all-alarms to set every currently raised alarm, or alarm-id-list to name from 1 up to 10 alarm ids (leafref). acknowledge-text is optional and stores a string of length 0..256 in the alarm itself. Setting an alarm to the state it already has is accepted, with only the text being updated. Example: set-alarm-state ack all-alarms acknowledge-text=example, or set-alarm-state ack 28872914984089790,17580406225060810165.

Yes: clear [-f] statistics [target=]<value>[,<value>]*, in Operational Mode. target is an instance-identifier naming the objects that will have their event counter statistics cleared. Currently the only supported object type is aaa-server, and AAA statistics are supported for TACACS+ servers but not for RADIUS servers. Clear every AAA server with clear statistics aaa-server, or a single one with clear statistics aaa-server-MyServer. The -f flag forces the command without confirmation and -h displays help.

Use show [-n=<number>] [-t] log [<logname> [exclude=<exclude-column> ...]]. -n=x displays only the last x entries and -t gives an aligned table instead of the default CSV output, for example show -n=5 log security -t. If the table becomes too wide, drop columns with exclude=<column> after the logname (tab auto-complete lists the removable columns), and post-process with piped commands, e.g. show log security | exclude john | include NETCONF. Valid logname values are messages, linecard, shell-command, netconf-command, apps, cli-command, alarm, configuration, kernel, user, event, security and ztp. Access mode is Operational, and Candidate Configuration for the show command only. Note that due to system restrictions the security log may not be cleared.

Yes, that is expected: console logging is off by default. The log-console attribute enabled (values true, false) defaults to false. Switch it on with set log-console enabled true, in Operational or Candidate Configuration mode, and verify with show log-console. The other log-console attribute is source-facilities, the list of syslog facilities used in this configuration: all, authentication, clock-daemon-15, clock-daemon-9, ftp-daemon, kernel, line-printer, local1, local2, local3, local4, local5, local6, local7, log-alert, log-audit, mail-system, network-news, ntp, security, syslog-internal, system-daemons, user-level, uucp. Severity filtering is then done with log-console-facility-filter.

Add a log-console-facility-filter: add log-console-facility-filter-<name> [severity <value>] [compare-op <value>], where <name> identifies a single syslog facility or all of them if it is 'all'. severity takes emergency (level 0), alert (1), critical (2), error (3), warning (4), notice (5), informational (6) or debug (7), and defaults to informational. compare-op takes equals, equals-or-higher or not-equals, default equals-or-higher. So to keep only serious messages: add log-console-facility-filter-all severity 'critical', which with the default equals-or-higher passes critical, alert and emergency. set, show and delete use the same key. Access: Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

It is set per log file with log-file. number-of-files is the maximum number of log files retained: uint8, range 1..20, default 10. When rotating files because max size is reached, the oldest files are discarded once the total number exceeds this value. max-file-size is the maximum file size before rotation in megabytes: uint8, range 1..30, default 30. So a default file holds 10 files of 30 MB, and the largest possible history is 20 files of 30 MB. Change them with add/set log-file-<name> number-of-files <value> max-file-size <value>. Other attributes are source-facilities (default all), pattern-match (regex, string 0..255) and sensitive-data (none, both, only). The default system log file cannot be edited or deleted.

Yes. Restrict the file's source-facilities to the authentication facility (facility 4, used for authentication/authorization attempt messages), then optionally add a severity filter. For example: add log-file-authlog source-facilities authentication, then add log-file-facility-filter-authlog/authentication severity <value> compare-op <value>. The filter key is add log-file-facility-filter-<log-file-name>/<log-file-facility-filter-name>, where the filter name is one syslog facility or 'all'. severity values are emergency, alert, critical, error, warning, notice, informational (default) and debug; compare-op values are equals, equals-or-higher (default) and not-equals. Note the log-file source-facilities default is all, so it must be set explicitly to authentication.

Configure the collector with add log-server-<name> address <IP address> ... transport <udp|tls|tcp> port <value>. Unless you say otherwise, transport is udp (so tls must be set explicitly), port is 514 (range 1..65535) and message-format is rfc5424, the alternative being rfc3164. Other defaults: enabled true, message-coalescence true, origin manual (or dhcp), source-facilities all, destination-facility-override disabled (otherwise a facility number in range 0..11 or 16..23), sensitive-data none (also only, both) and alarm-report-control allowed. name is a string 0...64, address may be IPv4, IPv6 or a DNS domain name, and pattern-match is a regular expression string 0..255. Access: Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

Yes, per collector, but it can only narrow. Use add log-server-facility-filter-<log-server-name>/<log-server-facility-filter-name> [severity <value>] [compare-op <value>]. The filter is based on the log-server source-facilities leaf-list and can only add a filter to the configured source facilities, so it cannot widen what the server sends; to add a facility you must change the log-server source-facilities. The filter name identifies one syslog facility (kernel, user-level, mail-system, system-daemons, authentication, syslog-internal, line-printer, network-news, uucp, clock-daemon-9, security, ftp-daemon, ntp, log-audit, log-alert, clock-daemon-15, local0..local7) or 'all'. severity defaults to informational, compare-op to equals-or-higher (also equals, not-equals). Example: add log-server-facility-filter-server184/local2 severity debug.

set syslog remote-logging-switch false. That flag, when false, disables all remote logging destinations while leaving the configured log-server entries in place; it defaults to true. Check it with show syslog remote-logging-switch. Access: Operational or Candidate Configuration mode. Related syslog attributes and defaults: source-address (default localhost), log-file-message-coalescence (true), log-relay, which enables remote logging from a shelf controller to a node controller (default false), assignment-method both/manual/dhcp (default both), niap-compliant-logging (false), privacy-mode, the GDRP filter (false), alarm-report-control (allowed) and label (string 0..256).

The aaa-server shared-secret attribute is documented as String (length 0...128) with default sharedkey, and it is displayed as * when shown. The command note states that the maximum length of shared-secret is 64 characters, and any value more than 64 characters is denied with an error message, so 64 is the practical limit. Set it with add aaa-server-<server-name> ... shared-secret <value> or set aaa-server-<server-name> shared-secret <value>, in Operational or Candidate Configuration Mode. The server-name itself is a string of length 1...64.

No, that is expected behaviour. show aaa-statistics-<server-name> authentication-requests displays the number of authentication requests, and the guide notes that for TACACS+ the default authentication protocol includes both PAP and CHAP: the authentication requests counter tracks each retry and each authentication protocol attempted independently, so authentication requests may increase by 2 for each retry. aaa-statistics applies only to AAA servers that use the TACACS+ protocol. The other counters are connection-failures (which includes failures due to unavailable servers and timeouts), authentication-rejects, authorization-requests, authorization-rejects and accounting-requests. Reset them with clear statistics aaa-server-<name>.

The ACE action attribute defaults to drop, so an unspecified match is dropped; the permitted values are drop, accept and reject. Syntax: add ace-<name>/<sequence-id> [action <value>] [direction <value>] [protocol <value>] .... Pre-condition: an ACL must be in place before an ACE can be added, and at least one of source IP, destination IP, L4 ports, TTL or protocol must be provided. sequence-id range is 1-100 for AUX and DCN-B interfaces and 1-256 for the DCN-A interface; use multiples of 5 so rules can be inserted later. A maximum of 16 ACEs can be created on an ACL if both upper-port and lower-port values are specified, and adding another such ACE beyond 16 returns an error. Other defaults: direction input, protocol any, ttl 255, logging-action false, lower/upper ports 0.

Use add acl-<name> type <value> interface <value> [admin-state <value>]. type indicates the top-level type of ACL and takes IPv4 or IPv6, so IPv6 is supported, and it is required at add time. interface references the interface the filter is applied to and accepts 1-AUX-1, 1-AUX-2, DCN, DCN-B, DCN-2 or DCN-2-B; run add acl-name interface ? to list the available ones. An ACL can be added on the DCN-B interface when the DCN is operating in active-active configuration. name is a string of length 0...30 and admin-state is lock, maintenance or unlock, default unlock. show acl-<name> also returns oper-state and avail-state. Example: add acl-AuxV4traffic interface 1-AUX-2 type ipv4.

Yes: show access-control-list. It takes no parameters and is available in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode; it simply displays the access control list. For the individual objects use show acl-<name> [admin-state] [oper-state] [avail-state] [type] [interface] for a specific list, and show ace-<name>/<sequence-id> for each access control entry within it. Note that the node's data-model access rules are a different feature, viewed with show access-rule-list-<name> and show access-rule-<access-rule-list-name>/<access-rule-name>.

Create an access-rule-list bound to that group, then a deny rule inside it. First add access-rule-list-<name> user-group <group>, then add access-rule-<access-rule-list-name>/<access-rule-name> action <value> [sequence-id <value>] [module-name <value>] [path <value>] [attribute <value>] [attribute-value <value>] [operation <value>] [description <value>]. action is mandatory and takes permit or deny. path is the target object, an XPath of a YANG data node, notification or RPC, or an external command, max 255 characters, default *. operation is a bits value of create, read, update, delete, execute (default *), so use 'create update delete' to block writes. module-name defaults to * and description is max 256 characters. Example: add access-rule-1/rule path /ne/equipment/card operation create action deny. The system supports a maximum of 500 access-rules across all access-rule-lists.

The access-rule-list is processed in order as given by the sequence-id parameter: lower number ids are processed first, so the lowest sequence-id wins. sequence-id is a uint16 and can be changed over the lifetime of the list to re-sort entries; if it is not provided it is set to the currently used latest id plus 1, putting the entry at the end of the list. Scope a list to groups with the user-group attribute: add access-rule-list-<name> user-group <value>, a leaf-list of user-group names whose default value * is a match-all meaning the list applies to all existing user-groups. A maximum of 20 user-groups can be referenced. description is a string of length 0..256. Example: add access-rule-list-A user-group XY.

It is OSPFv3-specific. auth-key adds, edits, shows or deletes the pre-shared key used for OSPFv3 IPsec integrity protection. The instance key is add auth-key-<instance-id>/<ospf-area-id>/<ospf-if-name>/<spi>: instance-id is the OSPF instance ID (number, range 0..255), ospf-area-id is the OSPF Router Area ID, ospf-if-name references the interface in the OSPF area, and spi is a unique security parameter index for this SA (number, range 256..4294967295). key is the pre-shared key, a string of length 8..128, and type indicates whether the integrity key is ascii or hex encoded. Access: Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. Example: add auth-key-1/0.0.0.0/DCN/256 key abcdefgh12345678.

Set the global authorization mode to rules-only: set authorization mode rules-only. The mode values are static-only (only system defined static authorization rules), static+rules (the default: the system looks for a user configured access-rule first and falls back to system rules) and rules-only (only user defined access-rules; if no rule matches, the global defaults apply). Then tighten those defaults, which are only configurable when mode = rules-only: read-default (permit/deny, default permit; covers get/show and receiving notifications), write-default (default deny; covers create/update/delete) and exec-default (default permit; covers RPC invocation and other commands). Set all three to deny for a deny-by-default posture. show authorization also reports denied-operations, denied-data-writes and denied-notifications.

A user changes their own password with the operational-mode command password [old-password=<old-password>] [new-password=<new-password>]. Both the current/old and the new password must be given, this is supported only for local users, and a password may contain up to 200 characters. Run password with no arguments for the interactive form: it prompts for the old password, then the new one twice, without echoing, and Ctrl+C cancels. Inline form, usable in scripts: password old-password=Infinera4u! new-password=Infinera4us!; inline, the double-quote and apostrophe characters must be escaped with a backslash and the characters # ? | ; must be enclosed in single or double quotes. To reset another user's password, an administrator uses set user-<username> force-password-change true, which forces that user to change their password at next login.

show security displays the top level security container. It takes no parameters and is available in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. Beneath it, show security-policies returns the individual policy flags (secure-mode, strict-password-check, minimum-password-length, ssh-authentication-method, default-user-group, password history, AAA methods, SSH and TLS algorithm lists, console-user settings, CRL/OCSP revocation, and the read-only max-system-sessions and max-local-users), while the related security objects have their own commands: user, user-group, user-data, access-rule-list, access-rule, authorization, acl, ace, access-control-list and aaa-server.

Both come from security-policies. minimum-password-length is the configurable minimum length for user passwords: number, range 1..200, default 8; the length is verified against this policy whenever a password is changed. strict-password-check (true/false, default true) additionally enforces a minimum length of 8 characters, at least one lower case letter (a-z), one upper case letter (A-Z), one number (0-9) and one symbol, and forbids the user name being part of the password; when disabled only a minimum length of 1 character is enforced. For reuse, enforce-password-history-check (true/false, default true) ensures a new password cannot match any of the previous 5 passwords, and password-history-size sets the number of passwords stored for reuse checking: number, range 1..200, default 5. These policies only affect newly defined passwords.

Both are per-user attributes of the user command. max-invalid-login is the maximum number of consecutive and invalid login attempts before an account is suspended (locked out): number, range 0-255, default 5. suspension-time is the duration of the UID suspension following consecutive invalid login attempts: minutes, range 0 - 1440, default 5. Configure with set user-<user-name> max-invalid-login <value> suspension-time <value>. show user-<user-name> reports user-status, which reads lockout when the account is locked out due to unsuccessful login attempts, and failed-logins, the number of previous failed logins, which resets to zero upon a successful login. Lockout can also be turned off globally through the security-policies disable-user-lockout attribute.

show user-data shows the user-data container. It takes no parameters and is available in Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode; the guide lists no attributes for it. For the per-user detail use show user-<user-name>, which can return password, password-hashed, user-group, display-name, max-invalid-login, suspension-time, timeout, password-aging-interval, password-expiration-date, enabled, user-status, force-password-change, max-sessions, last-login-date, failed-logins, user-aaa-type, alarm-report-control and label.

Use add user-group-<name> [description <value>], in Operational or Candidate Configuration mode. name is the name of the group, a String of 1...64 characters; description is a long description of the user group, a String of 1...128 characters. Each user is associated with a list of groups and derives its permissions from them; users are attached to groups via the user-group attribute of the user command. Manage with set user-group-<name> description <value>, show user-group-<name> [description] and delete user-group-<name>. Example: add user-group-XY. The predefined groups shown by show user-group are EA (Encryption Administrator), MA (Monitoring Access), NA (Network Administrator), NE (Network Engineer), PR (Provisioning), SA (Security Administrator) and TT (Turn-up and Test).
